questions.title: How does the 'administrative record' limitation affect the scope of the appellate court's review?
questions.question_body: The court states that its review of the BIA’s decision is limited to 'the administrative record on which the order of removal is based.' As a student, I'm struggling to understand how this limits the court. If a petitioner submits a new, compelling piece of evidence during the appeal process that clearly proves they were persecuted, can the court ignore it because it wasn't in the original record provided to the IJ/BIA?

questions.title: What is the threshold for 'cumulative harm' when no physical violence has occurred?
questions.question_body: The court acknowledges that they consider incidents collectively because 'cumulative effects' can constitute persecution. However, they also say 'threats alone are insufficient.' In this case, the petitioners faced multiple threats, a kidnapping/murder of a colleague, and a physical confrontation with their son. If there is no 'lasting physical harm,' what specific type of 'offensive' harm must be shown to cross the line from 'stressful' to 'persecution'?

questions.title: How does the court distinguish between a 'central' motive and a 'tangential' motive in mixed-motive cases?
questions.question_body: I'm confused by the Nexus analysis. The petitioners were clearly involved in politics, but they were also involved in a property dispute. The court ruled the political opinion was 'tangential and subordinate' to the property dispute. What objective test does the court use to decide which motive is 'central'? If a persecutor is angry about both a person's political views and their professional actions, how can the court 'de-couple' those motives to determine the primary driver of the violence?

questions.title: Under what specific circumstances does a 'failure to report' to the police become a fatal flaw in an asylum claim?
questions.question_body: The court mentions that a failure to report to the government can 'undercut' a claim but is not necessarily 'fatal.' They also mention that an applicant can satisfy the requirement by showing that reporting would have been 'futile or dangerous.' What kind of evidence would the court require to prove 'futility'? In this case, since the officer told Jimenez that 'police officers were contributing to the problem,' does that count as sufficient evidence of a futile reporting environment?

questions.title: How does the court weigh 'national' reach of a persecutor against 'localized' threats for the safe relocation analysis?
questions.question_body: The petitioners argued they couldn't relocate because the persecutors were associated with the Colombian government (implying a national threat). However, the court found they could relocate because the threats were to 'move out of the neighborhood.' How does the court distinguish between a persecutor whose reach is limited to a specific city/neighborhood versus one whose reach is national? If the persecutors have ties to the President, isn't the threat inherently national regardless of where the specific incidents occurred?

questions.title: Why does failing an asylum claim automatically result in a failure of a withholding of removal claim in this context?
questions.question_body: The conclusion states that because the petitioners failed to meet asylum standards, they 'necessarily fail' to meet the higher standard for withholding of removal. I thought withholding of removal was a non-discretionary relief with a different legal standard. If the facts of the case are identical, why does the outcome have to be the same? Does this mean that in practice, if you can't prove the 'persecution' element for asylum, it's impossible to win withholding?
